summary.text: Take the counterexample candidate \(n=736>599\). An exhaustive finite search shows that 736 has no representation as a sum of at most four squares whose bases are all at least \(8\), so the largest possible least base satisfies \(a(736)\le 7\), contradicting the claimed strict inequality.

full_proof.text:
Let us make explicit what the sequence value means. For a positive integer \(n\), consider all representations
\[
 n=x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_m^2,
 \qquad 1\le m\le 4,
\]
where the bases are positive integers arranged in nondecreasing order,
\[
 1\le x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\le x_m.
\]
Each such representation has a least base, namely \(x_1\), and \(a(n)\) is the largest least base occurring among all these representations.

We disprove the conjecture with
\[
 n=736.
\]
First, this number does have an admissible representation: for example,
\[
 736=4^2+12^2+24^2=16+144+576.
\]
Thus the collection of admissible representations is nonempty. We will prove that no representation of 736 as a sum of at most four positive squares can have all its bases at least \(8\). It will follow immediately that every possible least base is at most \(7\), and hence that \(a(736)\le 7\).

We use the elementary residue facts
\[
 t^2\equiv
 \begin{cases}
 1\pmod 8,&t\text{ odd},\\
 4\pmod 8,&t\equiv2\pmod4,\\
 0\pmod 8,&4\mid t,
 \end{cases}
\]
and, for even \(t\),
\[
 t^2\equiv
 \begin{cases}
 4\pmod {16},&t\equiv2\pmod4,\\
 0\pmod {16},&4\mid t.
 \end{cases}
\]
Also,
\[
 736\equiv0\pmod {16}.
\]
Suppose, for a contradiction, that
\[
 736=x_1^2+\cdots+x_m^2
\]
for some \(1\le m\le4\), with every \(x_i\ge8\). We divide the argument according to the number \(m\) of summands.

First consider \(m\le3\). Let \(r\) be the number of odd \(x_i\), and let \(s\) be the number of \(x_i\) congruent to \(2\pmod4\). The remaining bases are divisible by \(4\). Reducing the sum modulo \(8\) gives
\[
 r+4s\equiv0\pmod8.
\]
In particular, reducing this congruence modulo \(4\) gives \(r\equiv0\pmod4\). Since \(0\le r\le m\le3\), this forces \(r=0\). Thus all the \(x_i\) are even. The congruence modulo \(8\) now says that \(s\) is even. Hence \(s=0\) or \(s=2\). If \(s=2\), then modulo \(16\) the two bases congruent to \(2\pmod4\) contribute \(4+4=8\), while every base divisible by \(4\) contributes \(0\). The whole sum would therefore be \(8\pmod {16}\), contrary to \(736\equiv0\pmod {16}\). Consequently \(s=0\), so every \(x_i\) is divisible by \(4\).

Write \(x_i=4y_i\). Because \(x_i\ge8\), each \(y_i\ge2\). Dividing the equation by \(16\) gives
\[
 y_1^2+\cdots+y_m^2=\frac{736}{16}=46.
\]
We now rule this out for each of \(m=1,2,3\).

If \(m=1\), this says \(y_1^2=46\), which is impossible; for instance, a square modulo \(8\) is only \(0,1\), or \(4\), whereas \(46\equiv6\pmod8\).

If \(m=2\), it says
\[
 y_1^2+y_2^2=46.
\]
The sum of two residues chosen from \(\{0,1,4\}\), the possible square residues modulo \(8\), can be only \(0,1,2,4\), or \(5\) modulo \(8\), never \(6\). This again contradicts \(46\equiv6\pmod8\).

If \(m=3\), then three square residues from \(\{0,1,4\}\) must sum to \(6\pmod8\). The only possible pattern is
\[
 1+1+4=6.
\]
Thus two of the \(y_i\) are odd and the third is congruent to \(2\pmod4\). Since every \(y_i\ge2\), each individual square is at most
\[
 46-2^2-2^2=38,
\]
so every \(y_i\le6\). The odd bases among integers from \(2\) through \(6\) are \(3\) and \(5\), and the bases congruent to \(2\pmod4\) are \(2\) and \(6\). Therefore the square of the latter base is either \(4\) or \(36\), while the sum of the two odd squares is one of
\[
 3^2+3^2=18,
 \qquad 3^2+5^2=34,
 \qquad 5^2+5^2=50.
\]
Adding either \(4\) or \(36\) to any of \(18,34,50\) never gives \(46\). This rules out the case \(m=3\), and therefore all cases with at most three summands are impossible.

It remains to consider \(m=4\). As before, let \(r\) count the odd bases and \(s\) count those congruent to \(2\pmod4\). Modulo \(8\),
\[
 r+4s\equiv0\pmod8,
 \qquad r+s\le4.
\]
Modulo \(4\), this forces \(r\equiv0\pmod4\), so \(r=0\) or \(r=4\). If \(r=4\), then all four bases are odd, and their squares sum to \(4\pmod8\), not \(0\pmod8\). Thus \(r=0\): every base is even. The congruence then forces \(s\) to be even, so \(s=0,2\), or \(4\). The possibility \(s=2\) is excluded modulo \(16\), because the two bases congruent to \(2\pmod4\) contribute \(4+4=8\pmod {16}\), and the other two bases, being divisible by \(4\), contribute zero. Hence only two possibilities remain:

1. all four \(x_i\) are divisible by \(4\); or
2. all four \(x_i\) are congruent to \(2\pmod4\).

We rule these out separately.

In the first possibility, write \(x_i=4y_i\). Once again each \(y_i\ge2\), and division by \(16\) gives
\[
 y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2=46.
\]
Modulo \(8\), four residues from \(\{0,1,4\}\) must sum to \(6\). If \(u\) is the number of odd \(y_i\), whose squares contribute \(1\), and \(v\) is the number congruent to \(2\pmod4\), whose squares contribute \(4\), then
\[
 u+4v\equiv6\pmod8,
 \qquad u+v\le4.
\]
The unique possibility is \(u=2\) and \(v=1\). Thus exactly two of the \(y_i\) are odd, exactly one is congruent to \(2\pmod4\), and exactly one is divisible by \(4\).

Since all four \(y_i\ge2\), any one of their squares is at most
\[
 46-3\cdot2^2=34.
\]
Hence every \(y_i\le5\). In the interval from \(2\) to \(5\), the only number divisible by \(4\) is \(4\), and the only number congruent to \(2\pmod4\) is \(2\). These two bases contribute
\[
 4^2+2^2=16+4=20.
\]
The two odd bases, each either \(3\) or \(5\), would therefore have to contribute \(46-20=26\). But their possible square sums are again
\[
 3^2+3^2=18,
 \qquad 3^2+5^2=34,
 \qquad 5^2+5^2=50,
\]
none of which is \(26\). Thus the first possibility is impossible.

In the second possibility, every \(x_i\equiv2\pmod4\). Write
\[
 x_i=2y_i.
\]
Then every \(y_i\) is odd. Moreover, because \(x_i\ge8\) and an integer congruent to \(2\pmod4\) cannot equal \(8\), in fact \(x_i\ge10\), so \(y_i\ge5\). Dividing the original equation by \(4\) gives
\[
 y_1^2+y_2^2+y_3^2+y_4^2=184.
\]
Since the other three squares are each at least \(5^2=25\), each individual square is at most
\[
 184-3\cdot25=109.
\]
Thus each \(y_i\le10\). Every \(y_i\) is therefore one of the odd integers
\[
 5,7,9.
\]
Let \(b\) be the number of the four bases equal to \(7\), and let \(c\) be the number equal to \(9\). The remaining \(4-b-c\) bases equal \(5\). Their square sum is
\[
 25(4-b-c)+49b+81c
 =100+24b+56c.
\]
For this to equal \(184\), one would need
\[
 24b+56c=84.
\]
The left side is divisible by \(8\), whereas \(84\) is not divisible by \(8\). This is impossible. Thus the second possibility is also ruled out.

We have now exhausted every possible number of summands from one through four. Therefore 736 has no representation as a sum of at most four positive squares in which every base is at least \(8\).

In any nondecreasing representation, if the least base were greater than \(7\), then it and all later bases would be at least \(8\), precisely the situation just proved impossible. Hence every admissible representation of 736 has least base at most \(7\). Since \(a(736)\) is the largest of these least bases,
\[
 a(736)\le7.
\]
Finally,
\[
 736>599.
\]
Thus \(n=736\) violates the proposed assertion that every \(n>599\) satisfies \(a(n)>7\). This is the required disproof.
